paragraphs.source_en: Few attempts have been made at the interpretation of places according to the paintings. As mentioned above, Mori (2000) proposed the funerary function of Uan Muhuggiag shelter based on the excavated burials and the paintings evoking dead bodies. Soleilhavoup (2005; 2007) proposed the shelters with "flying" figures or presumed drums being places of shamanistic activities. Other proposed interpretations from various authors (e. g. Hachid 1998; Sansoni 1994; Muzzolini 1995a) are general statements about sacred places or sanctuaries. Given the lack of excavations the ethnographic record is now considered in the attempt to interpret possible functions of the Round Head sites.

paragraphs.source_en: Supposing that the Early Holocene groups of hunter-gatherers had regular meetings, what site might have been suitable for such purpose? Virtually every painted site with enough space to gather a large community may be considered suitable for possible meetings. An example is Tin Aboteka on the Tassili Plateau, a stone city on a small hill above a large plain. Shelters adorned with Round Head paintings are facing the plain with a view of tens of kilometres distant. A wadi passing just under the hill connects this place to other sites. The open character of this site is evident at first sight–being situated on the hill and open to the valley, the shelters could have been seen from an enormous distance and could have served as a point of orientation in the landscape.

paragraphs.source_en: The first shelter presents an image of a row of at least four identical masks interpreted as a stylized antelope or mouflon head (Lajoux 1962). The first mask is carried by a male individual probably dancing, with halfmoon attributes exiting from his back and from the left armpit. Other halfmoons, isolated masks and a mouflon are next to the figure. The importance of this painted wall seems to have been highlighted by a regular semicircle of stones delimiting the area, which is about 15 metres at the largest point in front of the shelter, thus making a separate small space within the area of other shelters (Fig. 5-1).
